name: Cyber Resilience Act
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: obligations apply 2026-27; one readiness survey by an interested party
summary: The Commission forecast that mandatory security rules for connected products and software would cut the cost of cyber incidents for businesses by EUR 180-290 billion a year, against compliance costs of up to EUR 29 billion. The main requirements apply only from December 2027. An open-source industry survey in 2025 found low awareness and readiness, but no study has measured effects on security or costs.

indicators.objective: Secure products throughout their life cycle
indicators.indicator: Significant incidents caused by vulnerabilities; share of manufacturers with secure development life cycle; patch frequency and time-to-patch
indicators.evidence: Reporting obligations apply from Sept 2026 and main requirements from Dec 2027; no measurement yet. A 2025 survey found most open-source respondents unfamiliar with the Act and few manufacturers producing SBOMs.

indicators.indicator: Absence of product-specific national cybersecurity legislation
Share of products shipped with security information and secure-use instructions
Reduction in incident costs for businesses
indicators.evidence: Not evaluated; Commission report due 36 months after application.

indicators.target_or_baseline: up to ~EUR 29bn (market value up to EUR 1,485bn)

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact Assessment accompanying the Cyber Resilience Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2022) 283), SWD(2022) 282
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the Cyber Resilience Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2022) 283)
literature.headline: Incident costs for businesses reduced by roughly EUR 180-290bn a year; compliance costs up to about EUR 29bn; possible higher prices for users; SMEs more affected as manufacturers
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the Act to cut the cost of cyber incidents for firms by EUR 180-290 billion a year, against compliance costs of up to EUR 29 billion.

literature.citation: Lawson & Hendrick (2025), Unaware and Uncertain: The Stark Realities of Cyber Resilience Act Readiness in Open Source, Linux Foundation Research (with OpenSSF and LF Europe)
literature.title: Unaware and Uncertain: The Stark Realities of Cyber Resilience Act Readiness in Open Source
literature.venue: Linux Foundation Research (with OpenSSF and LF Europe)
literature.headline: Most respondents unfamiliar with the CRA (62% not at all or only slightly familiar), uncertain about deadlines and penalties; manufacturers rely passively on upstream fixes and few produce SBOMs; calls for funding, legal support and clear guidance
literature.summary_plain: A 2025 survey of the open-source community found most people knew little about the Act and many manufacturers were not ready.
literature.interested_party: Linux Foundation and OpenSSF represent open-source projects and member companies directly affected by the CRA

literature.authors: Christian Szedlak, Holger Reinemann, Stefan Hatzelmann
literature.title: Ensuring cybersecurity compliance: Assessing SME awareness and preparedness for the Cyber Resilience Act
literature.venue: Proceedings of the 5th Asia Pacific Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management (IEOM), Tokyo, September 2024
literature.method: quantitative survey: 673 responses from 416 SMEs, 160 large and 91 very large enterprises
literature.outcomes: CRA awareness and preparedness by firm size
literature.headline: Only 12.3% of SMEs were aware of the CRA compared with 83.5% of very large enterprises.
literature.summary_plain: A large survey of companies found that very few small firms knew about the Cyber Resilience Act, while most very large firms did; small firms cited skills shortages and unclear rules.
literature.quality: Large sample but self-reported awareness, sampling frame unclear from abstract, survey around adoption (before obligations apply).
literature.citation: Christian Szedlak, Holger Reinemann, Stefan Hatzelmann (2024), Ensuring cybersecurity compliance: Assessing SME awareness and preparedness for the Cyber Resilience Act, Proceedings of the 5th Asia Pacific Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management (IEOM), Tokyo, September 2024

literature.authors: Roosa Risto, Mohit Sethi, Mika Katara
literature.title: Effects of the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) on Industrial Equipment Manufacturing Companies
literature.method: structured survey (44-question questionnaire in one-hour interviews) of 12 companies: 7 large industrial equipment manufacturers and 5 partner/consultancy firms
literature.outcomes: anticipated CRA compliance challenges (secure development lifecycle, vulnerability notification, skills)
literature.headline: 9 of 12 participating companies (75%) were quite or very familiar with IEC 62443-4-1 and the CRA; key anticipated hurdles were secure development practices, meeting vulnerability-notification deadlines and cybersecurity skills gaps.
literature.summary_plain: Interviews with a dozen industrial machinery firms show they expect the hardest parts of the new cyber rules to be secure software development and reporting vulnerabilities on time.
literature.quality: Very small convenience sample (authors note no statistical inference possible); used December 2023 text; anticipated, not realised, effects.
literature.citation: Roosa Risto, Mohit Sethi, Mika Katara (2025), Effects of the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) on Industrial Equipment Manufacturing Companies, arXiv:2505.14325

literature.title: IoT & OT Cybersecurity Report 2025
literature.outcomes: CRA familiarity, compliance measures, SBOM adoption
literature.headline: Only 32% of 300 German industrial firms were thoroughly familiar with CRA requirements, 14% had launched extensive compliance measures, and 12% had an SBOM for all affected products.
literature.summary_plain: A survey by a security vendor found most German industrial firms are not yet ready for the Cyber Resilience Act, with few having a full software parts list for their connected products.
literature.quality: Vendor survey with commercial interest in CRA compliance tools; sampling method not disclosed; self-reported.
literature.interested_party: cybersecurity compliance vendor selling CRA/SBOM tooling
literature.citation: ONEKEY GmbH (2025), IoT & OT Cybersecurity Report 2025, ONEKEY whitepaper (3 September 2025)

literature.authors: Adrienn Lawson (Linux Foundation); foreword by Roman Zhukov
literature.title: 2026 CRA Awareness and Readiness: Structural Unreadiness and Stagnating Awareness for Global CRA Compliance
literature.method: survey of 843 respondents (second wave after 2025 report) plus security analysis of over 12,000 open source projects indexed on LFX
literature.outcomes: CRA awareness, deadline knowledge, SBOM practice, compliance expectations, private-fork costs
literature.headline: 66% of respondents remain unfamiliar with the CRA (62% in 2025); only 34% identify December 2027 as the full compliance date; SBOMs for all products stayed at 32%, and passive reliance on upstream fixes rose from 46% to 51%.
literature.summary_plain: A year after the first survey, most people building software still do not know the Cyber Resilience Act, and companies' preparation has barely moved.
literature.period_geography: 2026; global, with EU and North America breakdowns
literature.quality: Follow-up wave of the existing Lawson & Hendrick (2025) survey with new data; non-probability sample, broadened to more North American respondents, which may affect comparability.
literature.interested_party: Linux Foundation/OpenSSF (industry-funded open source foundation); co-produced with Balena, Ericsson and Revanite
literature.citation: Adrienn Lawson (Linux Foundation); foreword by Roman Zhukov (2026), 2026 CRA Awareness and Readiness: Structural Unreadiness and Stagnating Awareness for Global CRA Compliance, Linux Foundation Research / OpenSSF (June 2026)
